💡 Marimo Tip: Clean Water is Key
Keep marimos in cool water (15–25°C). Avoid direct sunlight and warm spots.
Squeeze and roll your marimo gently to maintain its round shape.
Use filtered or distilled water. Chlorinated water can harm marimos.
Marimos prefer indirect light. Too much sun makes them brown.
Don\'t overcrowd containers. Each marimo needs space to move freely.
Healthy marimos make tiny oxygen bubbles - this is a great sign!
In winter, marimos grow slower and need less frequent water changes.
Marimos grow only 5mm per year. Patience is key with these friends!
Large marimos can be gently split into smaller ones to share.
Swirl the water occasionally to help marimos move and stay healthy.

Everything you need to know about keeping your marimo happy
Tap water (let it sit 24h to dechlorinate) or filtered water. Avoid distilled water — it lacks minerals marimos need.
Every 1–2 weeks. In summer or warm rooms, change more often. Cloudy water = change immediately.
Gently squeeze the marimo under running water to flush out debris. Reshape it into a ball after cleaning.
A small pinch of aquarium salt once a month can boost health and give a subtle ocean feel — totally optional.
Indirect, low to medium light. A north-facing window or a spot a few feet from a window is perfect.
Direct sunlight — it turns marimos brown and can cause algae overgrowth. Even a few hours of direct sun can be harmful.
Fluorescent or LED grow lights on a 12h on/off cycle work great, especially in rooms with little natural light.
Brown patches, bleaching, or slimy texture. Move to a shadier spot immediately.
15°C – 25°C (59°F – 77°F). Marimos thrive in cool-to-room temperature water.
Move marimos to the coolest room. Add a few ice cubes to the water occasionally during heat waves.
They tolerate cool water well — marimos naturally live in cold lakes. Cooler water holds more oxygen, which they love.
Temperatures above 28°C (82°F) for prolonged periods — this can cause deterioration and smell.
Extremely slow — about 5 mm per year. A marimo 5 cm across may already be 10+ years old.
A marimo (Aegagropila linnaei) is a rare form of filamentous green algae that naturally grows into a sphere shape due to lake currents.
Found naturally in Lake Akan (Japan) and Lake Mývatn (Iceland). They\'re protected in Japan and considered a national treasure.
When a marimo gets large enough, it can be split by hand into two pieces. Reshape each half into a ball — both will grow independently.
With proper care, marimos can live for hundreds of years. The oldest known natural marimos are estimated at over 200 years old.
Usually caused by too much direct light or very warm water. Move to a cooler, shadier spot and do a water change.
Gently roll the marimo between your palms under cool water to reshape it into a ball. Do this after each water change.
Healthy marimos sometimes sink — that\'s normal! They may float after photosynthesizing (producing oxygen bubbles). Sinking doesn\'t mean it\'s unhealthy.
Change the water immediately. This usually means bacterial build-up. Clean the container and the marimo thoroughly.
Often a sign of insufficient light or rotting inside. Gently squeeze to check — if it smells, you may need to trim away dead parts.
In Japan, marimos are called \'Marimo\' (毬藻) meaning \'ball seaweed\'. The Ainu people of Hokkaido consider them a symbol of love and good luck.
You can sometimes see tiny oxygen bubbles on the surface — that\'s your marimo actively photosynthesizing! A great sign of health.
Marimos can be kept together in the same container. They don\'t compete and can even coexist with small fish or shrimp.
Unlike most plants, marimos don\'t root in soil. They get all nutrients from the water around them.
Lake Akan in Japan holds an annual Marimo Festival (October) where locals float marimos in the lake to protect them.
